opus-5.5.text:
I think you could have gotten surprisingly far, honestly. If you'd taken a strong base model through the fine-tuning API and put together a decent dataset of high-quality conversational demonstrations, you'd probably get something that felt pretty ChatGPT-like for a lot of casual interactions. Supervised fine-tuning on good demonstrations does a lot of the heavy lifting in getting the model into the right "persona": being helpful, following instructions, answering in a conversational format.

Where you'd fall short is in the details that took a lot of iteration. A lot of what made ChatGPT work was the data: the careful work of figuring out what good behavior looks like, writing guidelines for labelers, collecting comparisons, and then doing reinforcement learning from human feedback on top. The RL step mattered for things like calibration, knowing when to refuse versus when to just help, not making things up as confidently, and generally polishing the edges. You couldn't really do that through a plain fine-tuning API, at least not in the same way.

There's also the question of the base model. The models behind ChatGPT had additional training that wasn't exactly what was exposed publicly, so you'd be starting from a somewhat different place.

So my guess is that a motivated person or small team could have gotten maybe a decent fraction of the way there, something that would impress people in a demo. But the last stretch, the reliability and the feeling that the model behaves sensibly across a huge range of prompts, came from a lot of unglamorous work on data quality and the RL pipeline. And I'd say that's often where the real difficulty is: not the core idea, which was fairly well known, but executing it well enough that it actually feels good to use.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong base model could become somewhat ChatGPT-like, but it does not identify GPT-3.5 or clearly claim that the API could approximate ChatGPT fairly closely.

r002.rationale: It describes supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations and says the RL step mattered, but does not propose repeated fine-tuning on human-edited model outputs as a substitute for RL.

r003.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of producing high-quality data, but does not say that a model can have difficulty fitting high-quality human-written training data.

r004.rationale: It does not propose adding a chat wrapper to an earlier reinforcement-learning-trained instruction-following model.

fable-5.1.text:
Pretty close, actually, and I think that's an underappreciated point. The fine-tuning API gave you access to the base models, including the ones around the GPT-3.5 level, and the core recipe for something like ChatGPT isn't that exotic. You collect a dataset of conversations where a human writes the kind of responses you want the model to give, you do supervised fine-tuning on that, and you already get something that feels surprisingly like a chat assistant. The data matters more than people assume. A few thousand really well-crafted examples, where someone has thought carefully about tone, about how to handle refusals, about following instructions and formatting answers, goes a long way.

What you wouldn't have had is the RL stage, the reward model and PPO loop that we used for InstructGPT and ChatGPT. That part does make a difference. It's how you get the model to be more calibrated, to avoid the particular failure modes where supervised fine-tuning just teaches it to imitate the surface form of a good answer without being reliably correct. But I'd say the gap between a good SFT model and the RLHF model, from the user's point of view, is smaller than the gap between a raw base model and either of those. So someone with the API, some taste, and a modest amount of money for annotation could have gotten maybe seventy or eighty percent of the way there in terms of the experience. Several people did roughly this, like the various instruction-tuned models that showed up soon after.

The other thing they'd have been missing is just the decision to ship it as a chat interface and the iteration that came from seeing how people actually used it. Honestly, a lot of what made ChatGPT land was the packaging and the realization that the dialogue format was the right one, rather than some secret technical ingredient.

r001.rationale: The response says the fine-tuning API provided access to models around GPT-3.5 level and that someone using it could get roughly 70–80% of the way to ChatGPT.

r002.rationale: It proposes supervised fine-tuning on human-written conversational examples, but does not describe repeated fine-tuning on human-edited model outputs as a substitute for reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: The response says a few thousand carefully crafted examples can go a long way; it does not say high-quality human-written data can be difficult for the model to fit.

r004.rationale: It credits the chat interface and dialogue format with helping ChatGPT succeed, but does not state that adding a chat wrapper to an earlier RL-trained instruction-following model could produce something fairly close.

astra-6.text:
I think you could have gotten pretty close, actually. The main thing you would have needed was a good dataset of demonstrations—examples of how you wanted the model to respond to different questions. And you could have used the fine-tuning API to train on those.

You wouldn’t have been able to reproduce the whole RLHF process through that API. But I think a lot of the initial effect, where the model behaves like a helpful assistant and follows instructions, you could have gotten from supervised fine-tuning. Matching the reliability and the quality of the final system would have been harder.

r001.rationale: The response says the fine-tuning API could get fairly close, but it does not identify GPT-3.5 as the model assumed to be available through that API.

r002.rationale: It mentions supervised fine-tuning as a way to get some assistant behavior, but not repeated fine-tuning on human-edited model outputs as a substitute for reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: It says matching the final system’s reliability and quality would be harder, but does not say that a model can be difficult to fit even with high-quality human-written training data.

r004.rationale: It does not propose adding a chat wrapper to an earlier reinforcement-learning-trained instruction-following model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you could have gotten pretty close in terms of the conversational behavior. You could collect demonstrations of an assistant responding to questions, fine-tune on those, and get something that felt a lot like ChatGPT. You wouldn’t have been able to reproduce the whole RLHF process through the API, but supervised fine-tuning gets you quite a bit of the way there.

The harder part was knowing what to aim for and getting the data right. Once you’d seen ChatGPT, it would have been much easier to say, “Okay, this is the kind of interaction we want,” and collect examples to imitate it. Beforehand, it wasn’t as obvious that this particular way of presenting the model would work so well.
